Context
-------
Read .github/copilot-instructions.md first.

This closes out the demo. It covers these things:

  1. A minimal status UI served by the frontend
  2. Business metrics emitted via OTLP only (the "small C" demonstration)
  3. An operational event feed driven by Alertmanager webhooks
  4. The demo app's Kubernetes manifests, which do not exist yet
  5. A `hey`-based load generator
  6. Perses dashboards, running against an external Perses on the host
  7. The host-side scripts that tie it together
  8. Updates to scripts owned by earlier prompts

The metrics path is now FIXED and confirmed. Do not change it:

  SCRAPE PATH (primary)
    The app exposes Prometheus-native metrics at /metrics on :8080.
    Prometheus scrapes them via ServiceMonitor. Names are hand-picked
    and stable. This is the path the alert rules and most dashboards
    depend on.

  OTLP PATH — traces
    The app exports spans via OTLP to the Collector. Already done in
    prompt 1. Do not change.

  OTLP PATH — metrics (the "small C" demonstration)
    The app ALSO emits a small set of business metrics via OTLP, through
    the Collector, into Prometheus's native OTLP receiver. These are
    deliberately NOT exposed on /metrics. The point is to demonstrate
    that Prometheus 3 ingests OTLP natively alongside scrapes.

  KERNEL PATH
    Cilium and Hubble metrics are Prometheus-native scrapes via
    ServiceMonitor. Already done in prompt 3. Do not change.

Do NOT route scraped metrics through the Collector. Do NOT add a
prometheusremotewrite exporter. The OTLP metrics path exists ONLY for
the business metrics listed in Part 2.

This prompt edits files that belong to earlier prompts:
  manifests/alert-rules.yaml         (from prompt 4) — new rule
  manifests/alertmanager-config.yaml (from prompt 4) — second webhook
  scripts/break.sh                   (from prompt 5) — torpedo case
  scripts/preflight.sh               (from prompt 5) — new assertions
Make those edits carefully and add a comment at the top of each edited
file naming the prompt it originated from.

Part 1 — Demo UI
----------------
Amend app/cmd/frontend to serve a minimal HTML status page with an
operational event feed.

Requirements:
- Serve at GET /index.html. The existing / handler stays as the API
  path — do not change its behaviour.
- Single self-contained HTML file, embedded via go:embed. No external
  assets, no CDN links, no web fonts.
- Displays, in this order from top to bottom:

  (a) ALERT BANNER — a full-width strip at the top.
      * Empty and dark when no alerts are firing.
      * Coloured by the highest-severity firing alert:
          critical  #f87171      warning  #ffb454
      * Shows the translated event text in large type.
      * Pulses subtly when the state changes. A CSS transition, not
        JS animation. No seizure-inducing flashing.

  (b) SERVICE STATUS — the service name (frontend / api / backend) and
      the current /chaos mode, colour-coded:
          ok     #4ade80
          slow   #ffb454
          error  #f87171
          dns    #f87171
          torpedo #f87171

  (c) RECENT REQUESTS — the last 10, as a list: timestamp, HTTP status,
      duration ms.

  (d) EVENT FEED — the last 50 operational events, newest first. Each
      entry shows:
        * timestamp
        * a coloured severity dot
        * the translated event text
        * the source alertname in 11px mono underneath, at reduced
          opacity

- Polls GET /status every 2 seconds for all four sections. Add /status
  as a JSON endpoint returning the same data.
- Minimal CSS inline in the HTML. Dark theme matching the slides:
  background #0b0d10, body text #d4d7dc, accent #ffb454.
- No JavaScript frameworks. Plain fetch and DOM manipulation.

The purpose of this UI is that the presenter can put it on screen as a
"what the operator sees" view, next to the observability stack. It is
not the main demo surface. Keep it small but make the alert banner
unmissable — that's the beat.

Part 2 — Business metrics, OTLP-only
------------------------------------
Amend the app to emit the following metrics via the OTel SDK. They are
NOT exposed on /metrics. They travel OTLP to the Collector, which
forwards them to Prometheus's native OTLP receiver.

OTel instrument names use dots. Prometheus 3 materializes them with
underscores and appends _total for counters. This translation is part
of the demo — the presenter will point at it.

  OTel name                        | Prometheus name                      | Emitted by | Rate
  ---------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------|--------------------------
  torpedoes.detected               | torpedoes_detected_total             | backend    | ~0.3/s baseline; ~50/s in torpedo mode
  sonar.contacts.detected          | sonar_contacts_detected_total        | api        | every request
  surface.ship.contacts.detected   | surface_ship_contacts_detected_total | api        | ~1 in 3 requests
  submarine.contacts.detected      | submarine_contacts_detected_total    | api        | ~1 in 5 requests
  countermeasure.launches          | countermeasure_launches_total        | backend    | every request while in error mode

Requirements:
- One Meter named "demo" in internal/telemetry.
- All counters share the existing OTLP exporter — the same one used for
  traces. One exporter, two signals. Do not create a second exporter.
- The /chaos?mode=error handler must increment countermeasure.launches
  on each subsequent errored request. This is a deliberate demo beat:
  the failure has an operational signature, not just a technical one.
- torpedoes.detected: implement as a background goroutine that ticks
  at ~1/s normally, and at ~50/s when chaos mode is "torpedo". The
  observable rate is what matters, not the mechanism. This is what
  gives TorpedoDetected a meaningful threshold to fire on.
- Surface vs submarine ratio: surface contacts are the more common
  contact class, roughly 5:3 over submarine contacts at steady load.
  Implement with a simple modulo or rand.IntN — do not over-engineer.
- All instruments must have a unit where applicable.

Add a "torpedo" value to the chaos mode set. In torpedo mode:
  * the backend continues to serve requests normally (HTTP 200)
  * the torpedoes.detected background goroutine ticks at ~50/s
  * no request-level behaviour changes
The torpedo mode is a signal generator, not a failure. It fires an
alert without breaking the service. That distinction is deliberate and
the presenter will call it out.

Update values/opentelemetry-collector.yaml to add a metrics pipeline:

  receivers:  otlp (grpc 4317, http 4318)
  processors: memory_limiter, batch
  exporters:  otlp/prometheus  (otlphttp exporter)
  pipeline:   metrics: otlp -> memory_limiter -> batch -> otlp/prometheus

The exact OTLP HTTP endpoint path on Prometheus is version-sensitive
for the pinned release. Verify it against the documentation for that
version before finalizing, and record the verified path in a comment.
If the pinned Prometheus does not support native OTLP ingestion, fall
back to prometheusremotewrite and document the change in a comment.

Part 3 — Demo app Kubernetes manifests
--------------------------------------
The app's Deployment and Service manifests do not exist yet. Create
them under manifests/app/.

Deliverables:
- manifests/app/frontend.yaml   Deployment + Service
- manifests/app/api.yaml        Deployment + Service
- manifests/app/backend.yaml    Deployment + Service
- manifests/app/servicemonitor.yaml

Requirements for every Deployment:
- namespace: demo
- labels: app: frontend | app: api | app: backend
  These exact keys are load-bearing — CiliumNetworkPolicy selectors
  depend on them. Do not rename or add variants.
- containerPort 8080
- image pinned by tag AND digest, recorded in versions.lock
- env:
    OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4317
    OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: <frontend|api|backend>
- readinessProbe and livenessProbe on /readyz and /healthz
- resource requests: 50m CPU, 64Mi memory. No limits.
- annotations:
    policy.cilium.io/proxy-visibility: "<Ingress/8080/TCP/HTTP>,<Egress/8080/TCP/HTTP>"
  This is required for Hubble to decode L7 HTTP. Without it, the
  hubble_http_requests_total metric will not exist and the alert rule
  will never fire. Comment this in the manifest. It also means the
  webhook traffic from Alertmanager to frontend is visible in Hubble —
  worth knowing.
- annotations (cosmetic, for the Hubble UI and Perses panels):
    demo/role: "periscope watch"     (frontend)
    demo/role: "sonar processing"    (api)
    demo/role: "command & control"   (backend)

Requirements for every Service:
- namespace: demo
- selector matching the app label
- port 8080, targetPort 8080

ServiceMonitor:
- Selects all three app Deployments on port 8080, path /metrics
- Label `release: kps` so kube-prometheus-stack picks it up. Verify the
  exact label against the kube-prometheus-stack values from prompt 3 —
  if the selector differs, match it and comment why.
- namespace: demo

Part 4 — Load generator
-----------------------
Create manifests/loadgen.yaml — a Kubernetes Job running `hey` against
frontend at a steady rate for a long duration.

Specification:
- Image: pinned by tag and digest in versions.lock. Use the official
  rakyll/hey image if one is published. If not, build a tiny image that
  installs the hey binary at image build time and is then self-contained.
- Command:
    hey -z 4h -q 20 -c 4 -disable-compression \
        http://frontend.demo.svc.cluster.local/
- restartPolicy: OnFailure
- namespace: demo
- labels: app=pilot, role=loadgen
- resource requests: 100m CPU, 64Mi memory. No limits — it must not be
  throttled.
- The Job must be idempotent to apply: delete-then-create, documented
  in a comment.

Part 5 — Perses dashboards
--------------------------
Perses runs EXTERNALLY, on the host, not in the cluster. Write three
dashboards as YAML under dashboards/, applied against that external
Perses.

Datasources to define, all pointing at in-cluster services via
port-forwards that run on the host:

  prometheus  http://localhost:9090
  loki        http://localhost:3100
  tempo       http://localhost:3200

Dashboard 1 — dashboards/overview.yaml — "Demo Overview"
Panels, in this order:
  a. Request rate, by service (timeseries)
  b. Error rate % — same underlying query as the alert rule
     (5xx / total), timeseries
  c. p50 / p95 / p99 latency, single service (timeseries)
  d. Active chaos state (stat panel, from app_chaos_mode{service, mode})
  e. Business telemetry row:
       - "Torpedo detections"
         query: sum(rate(torpedoes_detected_total[1m]))
         description: "Emitted as torpedoes.detected via OTLP.
                       Prometheus materialized the name."
       - "Sonar contacts"
         query: sum(rate(sonar_contacts_detected_total[1m]))
       - "Detection mix"
         query: sum(rate(submarine_contacts_detected_total[1m]))
                / sum(rate(surface_ship_contacts_detected_total[1m]))
         description: "Roughly 0.6 at steady load — surface contacts
                       outnumber submarines."
       - "Countermeasure launches"
         query: sum(rate(countermeasure_launches_total[1m]))
         description: "Moves only in error mode. The operational
                       response to the failure."

Dashboard 2 — dashboards/network.yaml — "Network"
Panels:
  a. hubble_http_requests_total by destination_workload, 5xx filtered
  b. hubble_http_requests_total by destination_workload, all statuses
  c. hubble_dns_queries_total by response code
  d. hubble_drop_total by reason (verify the metric exists under your
     pinned Cilium version; comment if it does not)
Titles and descriptions must name Cilium/Hubble as the source. This is
important — the dashboard should say out loud that the network is the
data source.

Dashboard 3 — dashboards/signals.yaml — "One incident, four layers"
Four panels side by side, all filtered to the same 5-minute window:
  a. Metrics: p99 latency
  b. Network: hubble_http_requests_total 5xx rate
  c. Traces: trace count by service (Tempo datasource)
  d. Logs: log volume by level (Loki datasource)
Description on each: one sentence naming the question that layer
answers.

Every dashboard YAML must:
- Use explicit datasources, by name.
- Have a stable metadata.name matching the filename.
- Be idempotent to apply via `persescli apply`.
- Be free of hardcoded timestamps or absolute time ranges.
- Use relative time ranges only (last 15m, last 1h) so they work
  whenever the demo runs.

Part 6 — Host-side scripts
--------------------------
scripts/40-perses.sh
  Starts Perses on the host as a container:
  - Bind to localhost only, port 8080.
  - Mount dashboards/ read-only.
  - Mount the plugins directory from bundle/perses-plugins/.
  - Apply the three dashboards on start.
  - Idempotent: kill any existing container, then start fresh.
  - Print the URL on success: http://localhost:8080

scripts/41-perses-portforwards.sh
  Runs, in the background:
    kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus-operated 9090:9090 -n observability
    kubectl port-forward svc/loki-gateway 3100:3100 -n observability
    kubectl port-forward svc/tempo 3200:3200 -n observability
  Writes their PIDs to /tmp/perses-pf/{prometheus,loki,tempo}.pid.
  Idempotent: kill existing PIDs from those files first.

scripts/loadgen-restart.sh
  Deletes and re-creates the loadgen Job. Called by break.sh baseline
  so the demo always starts from a clean state.

Part 7 — Updates to existing scripts
------------------------------------
# From prompt 5: scripts/break.sh
Update the baseline case to also run loadgen-restart.sh.

Add a torpedo case:
    break.sh torpedo  -> call /chaos?mode=torpedo on backend
The torpedo mode is a signal generator, not a failure. Its echo line
must say so explicitly:
    "backend: torpedo contacts spiking — no request impact"

Update the ok case to also reset torpedo mode on backend.

# From prompt 5: scripts/preflight.sh
Add assertions:
- Perses responds at http://localhost:8080/api/health
- All three port-forward PIDs exist and their processes are alive
- The loadgen Job is present and its pod is Running
- Prometheus returns a non-zero value for torpedoes_detected_total:
    curl -fsS 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=torpedoes_detected_total' \
      | grep -q '"value"' || {
        echo "✗ torpedoes_detected_total not in Prometheus — OTLP metrics path broken"
        exit 1
      }
- The webhook receiver accepts a synthetic payload and returns 200:
    curl -fsS -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook/alertmanager \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d @scripts/preflight-test-payload.json
  Add scripts/preflight-test-payload.json — a well-formed Alertmanager
  payload with one firing alert named PreflightTest.
  Then assert the event appears in /status:
    curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/status | grep -q 'PreflightTest'

Part 8 — Documentation
----------------------
docs/metrics-path.md must explain:
- The scrape path (app request metrics via ServiceMonitor)
- The OTLP path (traces and the business metrics via Collector)
- The kernel path (Cilium/Hubble via ServiceMonitor on the agent)
- Which metric name in the dashboards came from which path
- The dot-to-underscore and _total translation, with the narration line:
    "This metric never touched the scrape path. It was emitted as
     torpedoes.detected, travelled OTLP through the Collector, and
     Prometheus 3 materialized it as torpedoes_detected_total. The
     _total suffix is Prometheus's translation of an OTel counter."
- The countermeasure tie-in: in error mode, the failure has an
  operational signature, not just a technical one.

docs/alerting-events.md must explain:
- The full path from application event to operator UI:
    app metric -> Prometheus -> alert rule -> Alertmanager ->
    webhook -> frontend receiver -> translation -> UI event feed
- The translation table (see Part 9)
- Why the receiver is designed to pass through unmapped alert names
  unchanged, and what that means operationally (add a rule, get it in
  the UI with no code change)
- The torpedo mode: a signal generator that fires an alert without
  breaking the service, and why that distinction matters

Part 9 — Webhook receiver and event feed
----------------------------------------
Add a webhook receiver to frontend, and the alert rules that feed it.

# 9a. Receiver code

Add an internal package at app/internal/alerts with:

  translate.go   alert name -> operational text mapping
  store.go       a bounded in-memory event store
  webhook.go     the HTTP handler

The Event type:
  Timestamp    time.Time  `json:"ts"`
  Severity     string     `json:"severity"`     // critical | warning | ok
  Text         string     `json:"text"`         // translated, human-readable
  AlertName    string     `json:"alertname"`
  Status       string     `json:"status"`       // firing | resolved
  Fingerprint  string     `json:"fingerprint,omitempty"`
  Summary      string     `json:"summary,omitempty"`  // from annotations

The translation table, as a var:
  "DemoHighErrorRate": "Contact lost — elevated error rate"
  "TorpedoDetected":   "TORPEDO DETECTED"
Unmapped alert names pass through as the alertname itself, with
severity "warning". This is deliberate: adding an alert rule should
surface it in the UI with no code change.

Resolved alerts are prefixed with "CLEAR — " and severity "ok".

The store:
- Bounded ring buffer, capacity 50.
- Newest first on read.
- Safe for concurrent use. The webhook handler and the /status handler
  run on different goroutines.
- No persistence. This is an operator view of recent events, not a log.

The webhook handler:
- Path: POST /webhook/alertmanager
- Content-Type must be application/json. Reject otherwise with 415.
- Body size limit: 1MB. Reject with 413 beyond that.
- Parse the standard Alertmanager webhook payload:
    { "status": "...", "alerts": [ { "status", "labels",
      "annotations", "startsAt", "fingerprint" }, ... ] }
  Parse defensively. A malformed payload logs a warning and returns 400.
  It must never panic and never crash the process.
- For each alert in the payload, translate and append to the store.
- Return 200 with an empty body on success.
- Log one line per received notification with the alert count.

The /status endpoint must include:
  "events": [ ... the event feed, newest first ... ]
in addition to the existing fields.

# 9b. Alertmanager configuration

Edit manifests/alertmanager-config.yaml (from prompt 4).

The existing echo receiver must now have TWO webhook URLs:

  receivers:
    - name: echo
      webhook_configs:
        - url: http://echo-sink.demo.svc.cluster.local:8080/alerts
        - url: http://frontend.demo.svc.cluster.local:8080/webhook/alertmanager

The echo sink is NOT removed. Beat 3 of the demo shows the raw JSON
payload in the echo sink logs. The frontend receiver shows the
translated operational event. Both run from the same notification.

# 9c. New alert rule

Edit manifests/alert-rules.yaml (from prompt 4). Add a second rule to
the same group:

  - alert: TorpedoDetected
    expr: sum(rate(torpedoes_detected_total[1m])) > 5
    for: 30s
    labels:
      severity: critical
      pillar: business
    annotations:
      summary: "Torpedo contact — detection rate above threshold"
      description: "Source: OTLP business metric from the application.
                    No scrape path."

Threshold rationale: baseline is ~0.3/s. Torpedo mode is ~50/s. A
threshold of 5/s fires only in torpedo mode, with a wide margin. Do
not tune this without re-measuring both rates.

The `for: 30s` is shorter than DemoHighErrorRate's `for: 1m`, and that
is deliberate — the presenter uses the two rules to show that `for` is
a per-alert decision about how much tolerance you have, not a global
setting.

Constraints
-----------
- Do not change the metrics ingestion architecture.
- Do not add a prometheusremotewrite exporter unless the pinned
  Prometheus cannot do native OTLP, and document it if you do.
- Do not remove the echo sink or its receiver entry.
- Do not modify the CiliumNetworkPolicy or the Slidev deck.
- Every image pinned by tag and digest, recorded in versions.lock.
- Everything must work with the network interface down, except the
  initial build.

Acceptance
----------
1. curl http://frontend.demo.svc.cluster.local/index.html returns the
   HTML page. Opened in a browser, it renders and polls /status
   successfully, showing live data within 4 seconds.
2. The loadgen Job is Running. `hubble observe --namespace demo --last 10`
   shows steady HTTP flows at roughly the expected rate.
3. `curl localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=torpedoes_detected_total`
   returns a non-zero value. Paste the raw response into
   docs/metrics-path.md as a reference.
4. `curl localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=app_chaos_mode` returns a
   value. Paste the raw response into docs/metrics-path.md.
5. All three Perses dashboards load in the UI with no error banner and
   no empty panel after 30 seconds.
6. `preflight.sh` passes clean, including the synthetic webhook test.
7. Run `./break.sh errors`, wait 30 seconds, and confirm
   countermeasure_launches_total is increasing. Then `./break.sh ok`
   and confirm it stops. Report both observations.
8. Run `./break.sh torpedo`. Within 60 seconds:
     - TorpedoDetected appears as Firing in Alertmanager
     - `kubectl logs deploy/echo-sink -n demo` shows the raw payload
     - `curl http://frontend.demo.svc.cluster.local/status` shows an
       event with text "TORPEDO DETECTED" and severity "critical"
   Report all three.
9. Then `./break.sh ok`. Within 2 minutes a second event appears with
   text "CLEAR — TORPEDO DETECTED" and severity "ok". Report it.
10. Confirm the frontend container did not restart during either test:
    `kubectl -n demo get pods -l app=frontend -o json | \
      jq '.items[0].status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'`
    Must be 0.
